## Arms, Wrists, Preload, and the Meaning of Slack {#sec-lay-ch14}

## A Concrete Picture

Turn a two-hand valve. One strategy uses the arms to create most of the opposing
push-pull while the wrists remain firm. Another uses wrist moments more directly
while the arms stabilize. The valve can receive the same net turning effect in
both cases, but the loads inside the person differ.

Now reverse the motion. Motion reversal need not reverse the applied torque: a
continuing torque can first brake one direction and then accelerate the other.
A gear train that stays loaded against one tooth face avoids traversing backlash.
That does not make torque tracking instantaneous; compliance and actuator dynamics
can still delay the response. Reversing the load can instead require crossing a
gap before the opposite face engages. Biological tissue is not a gearbox, but
the picture creates a testable
question: does maintaining preload and load direction reduce a measurable
transmission delay compared with complete role reversal?

![Commands and Transmitted Torques in the Declared Synthetic Preload Experiment.](figures/proximal_distal_companion/fig_companion_preload_role_reversal.svg){#fig-lay-preload-reversal width=98% fig-alt="Solid lines show archived transmitted arm and wrist torque; dashed lines show commands. Both programs start relaxed at minus 180 milliseconds. At zero, persistent commands change from 10 and minus 4 to 16 and minus 6 newton metres; reversal changes from minus 4 and 10 to the same final commands."}

## How the Mechanism Works

The first experiment matches a **scalar control contribution**, not the entire
club task. At a fixed configuration and velocity, the constrained dynamics give
an affine acceleration map. Subtracting the zero-control solution leaves a
linear control contribution. The planar target is

$$
I_C\bigl[\ddot\alpha(u)-\ddot\alpha(0)\bigr]=8\ \mathrm{N\,m},
$$

where $I_C$ is club rotational inertia and $\alpha$ is club angle. The drift
acceleration $\ddot\alpha(0)$ remains part of the total motion. Proximal-only and
wrist-only generalized controls can each attain this increment at the sampled
states. Their convex mixtures attain it too, because this fixed-state map is
linear. Feasibility under strength, contact, activation, or other constraints
requires a separate check; the algebra alone does not establish human capacity.

Equal turning moment does **not** mean equal wrench. A planar wrench includes two
force components as well as moment about a specified point. Equal moments can
accompany different resultant forces, club translation, and work. For example,
adding the same transverse force at two symmetrically placed contacts changes
the resultant without changing their combined moment about the midpoint. Even
matching a complete wrench would leave some internal allocations undetermined.

The study varies 19 club angles and 21 mixture fractions. Its reported hand-force
RMS is calculated from the **control-induced contact-force increments**, not
complete measured hand loads. Its generalized-torque norm is an unweighted
Euclidean norm in the declared actuator coordinates; it is neither muscle effort
nor metabolic cost. Changing coordinate scaling or cost weights changes the
meaning of a minimum-norm allocation.

The labels *arm channel* and *wrist channel* identify generalized actuator
subspaces. A wrist control can also induce contact forces through the closed
chain; it does not isolate a pure contact moment from every other effect. Zero
direct wrist actuation does not imply zero passive wrist resistance or zero
constraint reaction. These results do not identify scapular retraction, muscle
activation, or a preferred technique.

### Two Extreme Stories

At one end, proximal arm-chain action creates the grip couple while wrists supply
resistance or impedance. The same general proximal drive can continue across
backswing and early downswing while signs remain loaded. At the other end, wrist
moments create more of the backswing couple while arms resist; during downswing,
roles reverse so arm-generated couple becomes positive and wrist action opposes
release.

These are useful poles, not a binary classification of golfers. Real allocations
can lie between them and vary continuously through time. The comparison asks
what each pole predicts under matched tasks.

### Replace “Slack” With Measured Variables

Slack can mean tendon slack length, grip gap, low muscle activation, low tangent
stiffness, joint laxity, series-elastic extension, or a delay in force rise.
Those are not synonyms. Having studied instantaneous allocation, we now ask a
different question: how does an internal transmission state affect the response
to a changing command? This second experiment uses two abstract channels,
each with deflection $x$, commanded torque $\tau^*$, stiffness $k$, dead-zone
half-width $\delta$, and time constant $T$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x^*&=\operatorname{sgn}(\tau^*)\left(\delta+\frac{|\tau^*|}{k}\right),\\
T\dot x&=x^*-x.
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\tau=k\operatorname{sgn}(x)\max(|x|-\delta,0).
$$

For a zero command, $x^*=0$. The parameters are $k=600$ N m/rad,
$\delta=0.012$ rad, and $T=18$ ms in **both** channels. The dead zone has total
width $2\delta$. Deflection follows a first-order lag; torque is obtained through
the dead-zone law. This is a phenomenological transmission model, not a measured
activation law or a literal anatomical gearbox. It contains no calibrated muscle
energetics, and its tracking score cannot establish energetic efficiency.

### Continuous Preparation Matters

Starting at a loaded equilibrium would hide how preload arose. The finite-history
test starts both channels at zero deflection, applies preparation commands for
$180$ ms, then changes commands without resetting the state. Each pair is
(arm, wrist) in N m:

- **Persistent Directions:** Preparation $(10,-4)$; after transition $(16,-6)$.
- **Complete Role Reversal:** Preparation $(-4,10)$; after transition $(16,-6)$.

Both desired sums change from $6$ to $10$ N m. This scalar experiment is distinct
from the earlier fixed-state $8$ N m allocation experiment; it does not simulate
a complete anatomical backswing. Preparation lasts ten time constants, bringing
the state close to equilibrium without reaching it exactly. The figure plots the
archived transmitted torques alongside the commands, including the initial rise
from the relaxed state.

The reported score integrates **absolute net torque tracking error** over the
first $120$ ms after transition:

$$
J=\int_0^{0.120\,\mathrm{s}}|\tau^*_{\Sigma}(t)-\tau_{\Sigma}(t)|\,dt.
$$

It has units N m s, but is not signed angular impulse and is not work. Finite
preparation gives $J=0.0717151$ N m s for persistent directions and $0.1954089$
N m s for reversal. The calculation uses a $0.1$ ms forward-Euler step and a
trapezoidal error integral. These are synthetic model outputs, not estimates of
human delay.

Persistent directions have no post-transition zero-transmission samples. Reversal
has arm and wrist zero-torque occupancies of $11.5$ and $22.0$ ms, with the study's
one-step brackets $[11.4,11.6]$ and $[21.9,22.1]$ ms. These sampling brackets are
not total model-error or physiological confidence intervals. Occupancy counts
samples with torque magnitude at most $10^{-12}$ N m; it is distinct from time to
useful opposite torque. The corresponding first attainment of 10% of the
post-transition target in its new direction is $15.7$ and $31.1$ ms. From an
identical relaxed state at transition, both programs have identical future
commands and therefore identical responses ($J=0.2010714$ N m s).

### What the Zero-Dead-Zone Control Establishes

With $\delta=0$ and the **same $T$ in both channels**, the sum satisfies
$T\dot\tau_\Sigma+\tau_\Sigma=\tau^*_\Sigma$. Equal initial sums and future net
commands then give equal net responses, despite different component histories.
The registered 12-case grid combines half-widths $0$, $0.004$, $0.012$, and
$0.024$ rad with common time constants $8$, $18$, and $35$ ms. Its three zero-width
cases are equivalent within $10^{-10}$ N m s; the other nine favor persistent
directions on this score. This is a conditional result within the specified
family, not a universal allocation optimum.

Unequal channel time constants break the sum reduction even with no dead zone.
For equilibrium initial torques $(10,-4)$ versus $(-4,10)$ and the common final
command $(16,-6)$, the difference in net responses is
$14[\exp(-t/T_{\mathrm{arm}})-\exp(-t/T_{\mathrm{wrist}})]$ N m. It is generally
nonzero when the time constants differ. Thus the negative control isolates a
mechanism within this model and comparison; it cannot uniquely identify a human
mechanism from a similar trace. Removing the dead zone also leaves first-order
lag: no gap does not mean immediate command tracking.

### Compliance Can Be Useful

Eliminating all compliance is not an implied goal. Elastic elements can store and
return energy; damping dissipates it. Compliance
can change peak loads, timing, and sensitivity, with benefits or costs depending
on the excitation and objective. None of those outcomes is measured by the
tracking score alone. The relevant question is which stiffness and preload suit
the task, including internal load and physiological cost, rather than how to
maximize rigidity.

The wrist-led extreme may reduce some proximal load, use elastic storage, or aid
participant-specific accuracy. The current objective does not price those
benefits. Its conditional continuity result therefore cannot select a universal
winner.

### What Must Be Measured

A serious human test needs bilateral six-axis grip wrenches and pressure,
closed-chain inverse dynamics constrained by those measurements, wrist and shaft
kinematics, shaft strain, transition-aligned force-development delay, and EMG
from forearm, shoulder, and scapular muscles. Perturbation or system-identification
methods should estimate tangent stiffness at a declared posture, activation
state, perturbation amplitude, and time scale. Dynamic impedance can also include
damping, inertia, and feedback. Preload is an operating load, not itself a
stiffness measurement. Holding out participants tests generalization; it does
not remove individual differences or justify prescribing a group average.

### Define Slack Operationally

Distinguishing these mechanisms requires different measurements: grip separation
can indicate contact loss, bilateral forces resolve load modes, and perturbation
response estimates stiffness. EMG and tissue imaging add complementary evidence
without directly measuring the net wrench. The transmission experiment alone
does not tell us which mechanism generated a measured trace.

A separate synthetic constitutive audit keeps five candidate mechanisms separate: contact disengagement,
transmission dead zone, structural preload, biological series compliance, and
control deadband. At the selected synthetic operating points, each class has a rank-three
local sensitivity matrix for its three fitted parameters under the registered
excitations. This concerns parameters **within an assumed class**, not selection
of the class itself, global uniqueness, or reliable estimation with noisy data.
Contact and biological surrogates have a normalized output RMSE of about $0.0196$
under the registered multisine, but that number is not a statistical detection
threshold. Their similar traces leave single-channel class identification
unestablished. This is a
useful negative result: a clean-looking force trace cannot by itself tell a
reviewer which kind of “slack” was present. Forward delivery and human tests
therefore need independent contact, shaft, tendon, activation, and bilateral
wrench measurements.

### Why Continuous Loading Might Help

Force does not appear instantaneously in biological tissue or actuators.
Electromechanical delay, tendon compliance, muscle short-range stiffness, grip
deformation, and neural feedback all introduce history. Maintaining some load
through transition might reduce the time required to develop a useful wrench in
the early downswing and could improve resistance to perturbation.

Continuous load could also require more co-contraction, raise internal load,
or constrain useful reorientation. These are proposed trade-offs to measure;
the two-channel model does not estimate fatigue or physiological cost. “No slack” is therefore not automatically optimal. The correct
question is whether a measurable loaded state improves a declared outcome at an
acceptable internal cost compared with alternatives.

### Why Role Reversal Might Help

Reversal can exploit different muscle groups and mechanical advantages across
phases. The backswing has more time and different geometry than the late
downswing. A wrist-dominant backswing allocation might position or load the club
efficiently, while proximal controls take a larger share of downswing drive and wrist
controls resist. That is a proposed allocation, not a measured anatomical
hierarchy established by this model. Antagonistic preactivation could also preserve
stiffness despite a change in net torque sign.

Therefore role reversal need not mean mechanical disengagement. Two opposing
preloaded torsional elements can exert $+5$ and $-5$ N m at equilibrium while
each contributes $100$ N m/rad of restoring stiffness: net torque is zero but
restoring stiffness is $200$ N m/rad. This illustrative construction is not a
fitted wrist model. Net moment can reverse while individual muscles or hand
contacts remain loaded. The experiment must measure force magnitude, differential modes, and
stiffness rather than inferring engagement from net sign.

### A Matched-Task Comparison

First state what is matched. Equal instantaneous angular moment, equal full
wrench histories, equal club trajectories, and equal terminal states are
increasingly different constraints; none follows automatically from the first.
Select a feasible comparison and report its tolerances. Under a matched scalar
task, compare the remaining wrench components as outcomes. If matching the full
wrench is feasible, compare joint demands, bilateral load distribution, work,
and robustness. Account for actuator limits and closed-chain consistency.

A second experiment can compare future evolution from matched configurations
**and velocities**, retaining different transmission states. Match other relevant
states and disturbances as well, or identify them explicitly as alternative
causes. Declare whether future commands or feedback laws are held fixed: freely
reoptimizing each program changes the causal question. Matching visible geometry
alone leaves momentum and several possible sources of divergence unmatched.

A targeted state intervention can test dependence on preload in a model, but
resetting a state may change stored energy, momentum, or constraint consistency.
Those changes and any physical preparation needed to realize the reset belong
in the accounting. If the entire deterministic state, future control law, and
external inputs are identical, uniqueness already implies identical future
motion. That equality is not independent proof of mediation. A convincing
mechanism test changes the candidate state while controlling competing pathways
and checks that the claimed effect survives feasible preparation and measurement
uncertainty. Chapter 15 develops the related shaft-memory problem.

### Predictions That Separate the Extremes

The continuous arm-dominant hypothesis predicts less force-rise delay after
transition, fewer or shorter near-zero-load intervals in the relevant bilateral
mode, and a particular sign continuity in arm-level control. The role-reversal
hypothesis predicts a clearer change in net allocation but may retain high
co-contraction or contact load. Both can predict similar club motion.

If a verified allocation change produces no practically meaningful difference
in the predicted wrench or stiffness mediator within adequately precise bounds,
that particular slack explanation loses support. Instructions alone do not
establish that an allocation changed.
If one allocation improves speed only by increasing peak load or face/path
variance, its practical value becomes conditional. If responses differ between participants, report that heterogeneity; subgroup
explanations should be prespecified or clearly exploratory and independently
tested.

### Safety and Coaching Boundary

This comparison is not an instruction to apply maximal opposing force or to
manipulate the wrists aggressively. The model does not estimate tissue safety,
and the linked EMG evidence does not identify a preferred strategy. Human
experiments require bounded tasks, clinical and ethics review where appropriate,
and monitoring of discomfort and load.

For a reader or coach, the useful principle is narrower: distinguish continuous
mechanical engagement from continuous net torque, and distinguish a felt cue
from the physical variable it is supposed to change. A cue becomes scientifically
useful only when it reliably changes the measured mediator and outcome.

### What Would Count Against Preload

The specific dead-zone account is weakened if its predicted contrast fails when
the declared model assumptions are reproduced; if an apparent advantage instead
comes from unequal channel dynamics, unmatched states, or a different control law; if measured transition load or stiffness does
not mediate the outcome; if continuous loading raises internal cost without a
robust task benefit; or if held-out participants show no repeatable relation.
These conditions prevent “connection” from becoming an explanation that fits
every result.

### Reader Lab: Make the Opposite Case Strong

Construct the strongest case for each allocation using the mechanisms above.
Separate what the declared transmission model predicts from the anatomical
assumptions that would need human measurements.

Write predictions that differ. Continuous loading should reduce a defined gap
in a particular force mode. Role reversal may show a sign change in allocation
without reduced stiffness. Both could yield equal club motion. Specify how
bilateral wrench, perturbation response, EMG, and shaft state distinguish them.

Now test a middle family rather than only endpoints. Map allocation continuously
from arm-dominant to wrist-dominant and allow phase-specific mixture. Plot speed,
face/path, load, robustness, and transmission measures. If an interior region
dominates both extremes, the spectrum has done its job by revealing that the
original dichotomy was too coarse.

### Interpreting a Null Result

If instructions produce no detectable allocation change, the experiment has not
established the intended contrast; inadequate measurement sensitivity is also a
possibility. It has not shown strategy equivalence. If allocation changes but a
well-resolved preload measure does not, the proposed pathway loses support. If
preload changes without a precisely estimated practical outcome, distinguish an
uncertain effect from one bounded below a prespecified useful size. A nonsignificant
result alone establishes neither absence nor equivalence. If the outcome changes
without the predicted mediator, examine competing pathways and mediator
observability before drawing a causal conclusion.

This staged interpretation prevents every outcome from supporting the same
story. It also respects participant differences: one subgroup may maintain
stiffness during reversal while another develops a measurable gap.

## Where the Picture Breaks

The gearbox picture is intentionally simplified. Muscle-tendon systems can have
slack-to-taut transitions and history-dependent behavior, but the chosen torque
dead zone and scalar deflection lag do not identify those biological mechanisms. Surface EMG cannot
measure force or stiffness directly. Scapular retraction does not map uniquely to
one hand force.

The model also treats two abstract channels, not dozens of muscles and joint
axes. Its numerical advantage is a conditional prediction awaiting data, not a
coaching instruction.

**Model Result:** Persistent load direction outperforms complete role reversal
on the chosen tracking score in the registered transmission family. Its
zero-dead-zone equivalence also depends on equal channel time constants and
matched initial net states and commands.

**Human Evidence:** [Kao et al. (1995)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7726345/)
recorded scapular-muscle EMG in 15 competitive male golfers and described
phase-dependent activity. [Robinson et al. (2023)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37983261/)
studied 15 sub-elite male golfers and found side-dependent wrist kinematics and
extensor carpi ulnaris EMG. Their reported lack of a significant relationship
between downswing EMG and impact clubhead kinematics is not an equivalence test.
Neither study identifies the bilateral wrench allocation proposed here. EMG is
an electrical measurement, not a direct measure of muscle force or stiffness.

**Hypothesis:** Proximal push-pull during preparation may preserve useful
transmission continuity while wrists resist, but the opposite allocation could
win on load, accuracy, or participant-specific objectives.

**Practical Interpretation:** “No slack” should become a measurement question:
was there a force gap, low tangent stiffness, delayed transmission, or merely a
different internal allocation?
